newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal receives key accused.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal receives key accused.

text.p: The U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal on Friday welcomed the boost to its credibility from the arrival for trial of Colonel Theoneste Bagosora, the most wanted former official in Rwanda so far indicted for the 1994 genocide.

Officials said Bagosora arrived by plane from Cameroon with three other indicted suspects at the tribunal's headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Thursday night and would appear in court in the coming days.
They would have to plead and trial dates would be set.
Bagosora was cabinet director in Rwanda's defence ministry at the time of the genocide and is accused of directing the first days of the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
The four were handed over by Cameroon to the tribunal after nearly a year in detention because of delays in President Paul Biya approving their transfer.

"The success of this operation proves, if proof be needed, that African governments and the entire international community are supporting and cooperating with the tribunal," the tribunal said in a statement.
Tribunal officials said the arrival of the four was a big boost for the tribunal, battered by delays in bringing suspects to trial and internal disputes including problems of staffing.
The tribunal has been shaken and its credibility threatened amid charges by some staff of racism in hiring, incompetence and nepotism which led to an an internal investigation by the United Nations.
Bagosora is widely regarded as the most wanted suspect so far detained.

The other three are Anatole Nsengiyumva, a former lieutenant-colonel, Andre Ntagerura, a former minister of transport, and Ferdinand Nahimana, a former director of extremist Radio Mille Collines, which fanned ethnic hatred during the killings.

"The four accused will be the first indictees before the International Tribunal in Arusha who during the 1994 genocide were very influential or held positions of national authority," said Chief Prosecutor Louise Arbour in a statement on Thursday.
"Their transfer markes a capital turning point for the credibility of the International Tribunal and demonstrates the tribunal's capability to prosecute the principal perpetrators," she added.
A total of 21 people have been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. The arrival of the four brought to 11 the number of suspects in its detention at Arusha.
The tribunal was set up in November 1994 to bring to justice the main architects of the three-month genocide in Rwanda of Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
Its maximum penalty is life imprisonment.
Rwanda started trials late last month of some of the 90,000 suspects crammed into its prisons and at least eight have already been sentenced to death.
The four accused who arrived in Arusha on Thursday are defended by lawyers approved by the tribunal's Kenyan registrar. Few of the accused to appear in Rwandan courts have any defence counsel.
